Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: GERD is a condition where stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing symptoms or complications [18]. The typical symptoms are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18]. It can affect quality of life and may lead to problems like erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, which can be a precursor to esophageal cancer [18]. In children, GERD is a less common pathological process causing troublesome symptoms, whereas simple reflux is often normal and managed without medication [19]. Factors that contribute to GERD include abnormal relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, defects in the esophageal lining's defense, impaired movement and clearance of the esophagus and stomach, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19]. In young children, the symptoms are varied and nonspecific, requiring careful diagnostic evaluation [19].

The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18#0]. GERD is a gastrointestinal motility disorder where stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing symptoms or complications [18#1]. It can lead to serious complications including inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, and Barrett esophagus, which can develop into esophageal cancer [18#2]. In children, GERD has varied and nonspecific signs that require careful evaluation [19#3]. Factors that contribute to GERD include abnormal relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, defects in the esophageal lining's defense, impaired movement and clearance of the esophagus and stomach, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#4]. These symptoms are among the most commonly reported to primary care providers [20#5]. While the most effective treatment is proton-pump inhibitors, long-term use carries risks including bone fractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, and intestinal infection [18#6][18#7]. The medical concept is recorded under the name Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) [2], and the entity name Gastroesophageal Reflux is also used [3]. Several clinical trials are studying GERD treatments, including famotidine for non-erosive GERD [4], pantoprazole for acid reflux symptoms in adults [7], on-demand treatment of reflux disease [13], and endoscopic fundoplication as a placebo-controlled study [16]. A trial is also examining the natural history of gastroesophageal reflux in children and adolescents [10]. Publications on GERD include PMID 29132520 [5], PMID 33351044 [8], PMID 36170502 [11], PMID 37034973 [14], and PMID 37516506 [17]. Additional published titles include Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [1], Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [6], Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [9], Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [15], and Gastroesophageal reflux disease in children: What's new right now? [12].
